qrdBas-a17109-d1e101.summary: Rubric for the seventh prologue question of Book 1.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e108.summary: States the question: whether knowledge is called practical first and principally from its order to praxis as end, or from its order to the object, or to praxis as object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e124.summary: First argument that practical knowledge is so called from its object: Metaphysics VI divides practical from speculative sciences by objects (practical concern things whose principles are in us), so knowledge is first practical from its object.
claims: Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by objects.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e146.summary: Second: Ethics VI distinguishes the object of the practical intellect, the doable contingent good, from the speculative intellect and habit. The last words introduce the opposing authority.
claims: The practical intellect's object is the contingent doable good.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e158.summary: Against: De anima III says the intellect becomes practical solely by extension to action as end, differing from the speculative by its end; so habit or act is practical first from the end.
claims: The practical intellect differs from the speculative by its end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e171.summary: Further: Metaphysics I (II) distinguishes practical and speculative by ends, truth for speculative, work for practical. The paragraph ends by announcing the order of procedure.
claims: Speculative science aims at truth, practical at work.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e182.summary: First step: declare what praxis is and draw conclusions.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e189.summary: Second step: show whether intellect and habit or act are called practical from the same thing.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e194.summary: Third step: from what a habit is first and principally called practical, end or object, and how.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e201.summary: Fourth step: whether speculative and practical are essential differences of intellect and habit.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e209.summary: Fifth step: respond to the principal arguments. The last words begin the definition of praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e216.summary: Defines praxis, from which knowledge is called practical: an operation of a power other than the intellect, of another genus than cognition, not of its nature ordered to generating cognition (as instrument, path, or disposition), naturally posterior to intellection, in the power of the knower, apt to be directed by right reason, and the per se, intrinsic, proper, and principal end of the directive knowledge or science.
claims: Praxis is an operation of a non-intellectual power, posterior to and directable by intellection, in the knower's power, and the per se end of directive knowledge.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e238.summary: First condition, that praxis belongs to another power than the intellect: the intellect is said to extend outside itself to praxis, but in its own operations it remains within. Otherwise logic, directing the intellect's discursive acts, would be practical.
claims: Praxis is an operation of a power other than intellect.
Logic is not practical, though it directs intellectual acts.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e264.summary: Second condition, that praxis is of another genus than cognition: it is not intellectual, belonging to another power, nor sensitive, since sensation is ordered to acquiring intellectual knowledge, so knowledge directing it would be speculative. Science is called practical from operation as distinguished from cognition (Metaphysics I-II).
claims: Praxis is not cognition, intellectual or sensitive.
Sensation is ordered to knowledge, so directing it is speculative.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e295.summary: Third condition, that praxis is not of itself ordered to causing knowledge: operations causing knowledge, like external speech, are ordered to knowing, and science directing them for knowledge's sake is speculative. Otherwise the linguistic sciences would be practical, which is false.
claims: Operations ordered to producing knowledge are not praxis.
The linguistic arts are not practical sciences.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e319.summary: Fourth condition, that praxis is naturally posterior to intellection: knowledge necessarily precedes it, showing its object and serving as the rule it must conform to in order to be right. Acts not posterior to intellection, such as vegetative acts, sensation, and sense appetite preceding reason, are not properly praxis.
claims: Praxis is naturally posterior to the intellection that shows and rules it.
Vegetative and pre-rational appetitive acts are not praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e346.summary: Fifth condition, that praxis is in the knower's power: the principle of practical acts is in the knower (Ethics VI). The artisan needs art and the moral agent virtue to act rightly, and no one needs these for what is not in his power, since art is an efficient principle (Physics II). In practical matters the knower has the active principle of the operation (Metaphysics VI), so practical sciences are called active or factive.
claims: Praxis is in the power of the knower.
Art and virtue are needed only for what is in one's power.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e379.summary: Sixth condition, that praxis is directable by right reason: it is an operation that can be right or not, so directive knowledge is needed, which would be unnecessary for what is necessarily right. The intellect understands itself and the other powers (Augustine, De trinitate XV) and can judge and direct their acts. So praxis presupposes intellection not only showing its object but as rule and measure to which it must conform to be right, as Ethics VI says right choice requires right reason, and likewise every act of will.
claims: Praxis can be right or not, hence needs directive knowledge.
Right reason is the rule and measure of right praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e431.summary: Note: it is not enough that knowledge show its object to be practical; it must also direct, else all knowledge would be practical and every act of will praxis. Praxis must be directable, else every operation of the will would qualify, since the other conditions are met. Arts like lyre-playing are posited for directable acts in which error is possible. Directive habits are practical principally because of the circumstances of the act, in which error is possible, not its substance.
claims: Practical knowledge must be directive, not merely ostensive.
Directive habits regulate the circumstances of acts, where error occurs.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e475.summary: Seventh condition, that praxis is the per se, proper, intrinsic, and principal end of directive knowledge. End: Metaphysics II, 'the end of practical science is work'. Per se: from the nature of the knowledge, not the knower's intention, else the same habit would be sometimes practical and sometimes speculative. Intrinsic: not that praxis must be elicited by the same power, as some falsely imagine (then the end would be truth), but intrinsic to the definition of the science. An extrinsic end does not make a science practical, else moral science would be speculative because its end is contemplative happiness; a remote, common cause does not determine a nature. Proper and principal: moral science's proper end includes knowledge of the doable good, but its principal end is operation of the human good ('that we may become good'). Moral science differs from prudence as art from experience, universal from particular.
claims: Praxis must be the per se end of practical knowledge by its nature, not by the knower's intention.
A practical habit cannot become speculative.
Extrinsic remote ends do not determine a science as practical or speculative.
Moral science differs from prudence as universal from particular.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e577.summary: This description of praxis agrees with a doctor's (Scotus's) shorter one: praxis is an act of a power other than intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason so as to be right.
claims: The description agrees with Scotus's definition of praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e590.summary: First corollary: praxis is only an act of the will, elicited or commanded, since only such acts meet all the conditions; any other operation has some of the same kind that can precede intellection, and only acts of will are in the knower's power and directable by right reason.
claims: Praxis is exclusively an act of the will, elicited or commanded.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e620.summary: Second corollary: the elicited act of will, willing, is first and per se praxis even when separated from any act of lower powers, as in willing God, where no sense appetite or motive power can act, yet all conditions apply. Aristotle (De anima III) posits higher and lower appetites; some think an act of the lower without the higher would be true praxis, which the author denies, but the higher's act without the lower is praxis.
claims: The will's elicited act is per se praxis even without any bodily act.
Willing God is praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e664.summary: Third corollary: no act of a power other than the will is praxis except in order to an elicited act of will commanding it, since the conditions apply to it only through that act. The paragraph ends by introducing the second article.
claims: Acts of other powers are praxis only as commanded by the will.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e680.summary: Second article: whether intellect and habit are called practical or speculative from the same thing. An opinion says no: the intellect is practical from the end, being moved by appetite for an end to consider means (it first apprehends the end, the will delights in it, wills it efficaciously, then the intellect considers means), and before that it is not practical. The habit or act is practical from its object, operable or not by the knower. Since operable and non-operable objects are formally distinct per se objects, they distinguish habits specifically, so the practical-speculative difference is per se and formal in habits but accidental in the intellect, whose object is being.
claims: The intellect is practical from the end, through the will's appetite.
Habits are practical from their operable objects.
Practical and speculative are essential differences of habits but accidental to the intellect.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e761.summary: Consequences of that view: considering an operable object without desire for the end yields practical consideration with speculative intellect; considering a non-operable object out of desire for an end yields speculative consideration with practical intellect; and so on for the other combinations.
claims: On this view intellect and habit can diverge in being practical or speculative.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e790.summary: Confirmed by De anima III (the practical intellect differs from the speculative by its end) and Ethics VI (the good of the practical intellect is truth in conformity with right appetite), so the intellect is practical from the end or appetite, but habits from objects (Metaphysics VI). The paragraph ends by introducing arguments against.
claims: The intellect is practical by conformity with appetite.
concepts: truth in conformity with right appetite

qrdBas-a17109-d1e812.summary: Against: either the intellect is taken as under the act or habit, in which case it is necessarily denominated from them and from the same thing, sharing the same object, end, and act, and the same presence or absence of appetite for the end; or it is taken nakedly as power, in which case it is neither practical nor speculative but simply intellect, one simple uniform power.
claims: Intellect under a habit is denominated from that habit.
The bare power of intellect is neither practical nor speculative.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e855.summary: Second: practical acts never generate a speculative habit, so a practical intellect never generates a speculative habit or conversely. If intellect is practical from the end and habit from the object, then by parity act could be speculative and generated habit practical.
claims: Practical acts generate practical habits; the same should hold for intellect.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e877.summary: Third: Metaphysics II says the end of speculative habit is truth and of practical, work; De anima III says the intellects differ by end; so both intellect and habit are practical from the end. And De anima III says the practical intellect's object is the doable contingent good, so it is practical from its object, against them.
claims: Aristotle derives the practical character of both habit and intellect from the end, and of intellect also from the object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e901.summary: Their reply: work is the end of practical science not per se but accidentally and potentially, insofar as it concerns an operable object considered universally, which does not suffice to subject the object to actual operation. Another particular habit and consideration in the practical intellect is required, generated from practical acts moved by appetite for the end. Since work is an end only potentially and accidentally, practical and speculative are distinguished by the per se operable object, not by the end.
claims: Work is only an accidental, potential end of universal practical science.
Practical science is distinguished by its operable object, not its end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e940.summary: Against them: if habits are distinguished by objects, a practical habit about an operable object in the speculative intellect and another in the practical intellect would be of the same kind about the same object, and one would be superfluous, since the will's relation to the end does not distinguish habits on their view.
claims: Their view yields superfluous duplicate habits.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e966.summary: Further: there would be two habits of the same kind in the same power, one generated from practical acts in the speculative intellect, one in the practical intellect moved by desire, which is false.
claims: Two habits of the same kind cannot coexist in one power.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e982.summary: Further: Aristotle speaks of the per se end of the practical intellect, not an accidental or potential one; as truth is the per se end of speculative habit, so work of practical knowledge, and he distinguishes them by per se ends.
claims: Aristotle distinguishes practical and speculative by per se ends.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1001.summary: Confirmed: in Metaphysics I Aristotle argues that a science for the sake of use is less noble, which holds only if use is its per se end. Though the author thinks the inference is invalid unless explained, it holds by Aristotle's judgment and intention, so use is the per se end of practical knowledge; the opponents do not hold to their Aristotle.
claims: Aristotle treats use as the per se end of practical science.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1023.summary: Further: a subject is denominated more from a per se condition of its accident than from an accidental condition; so if the intellect can be called practical from the accidental condition of the will ordering its act to an end, much more from the per se condition by which its habit is practical, whether order to object (on their view) or to end (on the author's).
claims: The intellect is more properly denominated from its habit's per se condition than from accidental relations to the will.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1043.summary: Conclusion of the second article: the intellect and its habit or act are practical from the same thing, whether object or end (to be decided in the next article), though the intellect is not called practical as per se or immediately as the habit or act.
claims: Intellect and habit are practical from the same source.
Intellect is denominated practical less immediately than its habit.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1069.summary: Third article: some (Scotus) say knowledge or habits are called practical principally from the object. Even if knowledge is called practical from praxis, this is not as end but as secondary object of the practical knowledge concerning its primary object, so that knowledge is practical because it extends or is extendible to praxis as object, not as end.
claims: Knowledge is practical from extension to praxis as object, not as end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1089.summary: First proof: an end causes only as loved and actually moving the efficient cause, but practical knowledge, and its extendibility to work, exists in the intellect however the will stands toward the end, even if per impossibile there were intellect without will. The reply that the end is apt to be loved fails, since aptitude does not make the end actually cause, and no effect is actual from a cause not actually causing.
claims: An end causes only as actually loved.
Practical knowledge exists regardless of the will's actual love of the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1120.summary: Second proof: the end makes knowledge practical either as existing in reality (posterior to the knowledge it is directed by, and the prior does not depend on the posterior) or as intended and loved (but knowledge is practical before the end is loved, and as loved or considered the end functions as object, not end). So knowledge is practical from the object.
claims: The end cannot make knowledge practical either as existing or as intended.
The end as considered functions as object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1145.summary: Third proof for the object view: if being practical were ordering to praxis as end, moral science would not be practical, since its end would be an act of moral virtue, some or all of which reside in the sense appetite, and an act of a lower power cannot be the end of an intellectual habit, being less noble.
claims: Acts of lower powers cannot be the end of intellectual habits.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1171.summary: Fourth: the object as object virtually contains the whole of practical knowledge, as the object of speculative knowledge contains its principles and through them its conclusions; so practical knowledge depends on the object, not the will or end, since the object contains it before the end is loved.
claims: The object virtually contains all practical knowledge prior to love of the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1191.summary: Fifth: habits are called practical by aptitudinal or actual extension to work or end. Not aptitudinal, since an aptitude is only a relation of reason, and nothing is actually such by a mere aptitude; and an aptitude belongs to one nature and not another only because of something absolute, which must come from a per se cause of practical knowledge (object, intellect, or end), and not intellect or end, since the extension belongs whether or not the end is loved; so from the object.
claims: Aptitudinal extension is a relation of reason founded on something absolute.
The absolute ground of practical knowledge must come from the object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1235.summary: Further: then extension would be actual, as effect to the cause giving its nature. Nor actual extension, else one not actually intending to act would lack practical knowledge, and a sleeping smith would lack his practical art, which is false.
claims: Actual extension would make a sleeping smith lack practical art.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1255.summary: Further: Metaphysics VI distinguishes practical from speculative because practical concern things whose principle is in the knower; so practical and speculative are taken principally from objects, operable and non-operable.
claims: Practical and speculative are distinguished by operable and non-operable objects.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1266.summary: Further: Ethics VI distinguishes the calculative part (practical) from the scientific (speculative) by objects, operable and non-operable.
claims: Ethics VI distinguishes rational parts by objects.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1278.summary: Further: Aristotle infers that if there is separate immobile substance, science of it is speculative, which holds only if speculative is taken from the object; so practical too, and not from praxis except as object. Likewise the practical intellect, as they say.
claims: Aristotle infers speculative character from the object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1298.summary: Further reasons for the object view: habits are specified by objects as acts are (De anima II); the object causes the habit in caused things, and praxis as end is caused by the object; habits would be speculative or practical even with ends removed; speculation and praxis themselves are distinguished by objects; the object is a more principal end than praxis, being end 'of which' rather than end 'by which'.
claims: Habits are specified by objects.
The object is a more principal end than praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1324.summary: Reply: acts are not distinctively specified by objects, since the same object can have distinct acts; De anima II speaks of the particular senses. The same answers the fourth.
claims: The same object can have distinct acts.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1337.summary: Reply to the second: though the object causes in caused things, it is not thereby more distinctive, being less determinate.
claims: The object is less determinate than the end and so less distinctive.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1344.summary: Reply to the third: with the end removed there would be no practical habit, as will appear below.
claims: Without the end there is no practical habit.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1351.summary: Reply to the fifth: the object of praxis is a more principal end, but less proper, less determinate, and less proximate under the conditions of praxis. The paragraph's last words begin the author's arguments against the opinion.
claims: The object is a more principal but less proper end than praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1365.summary: Against the opinion, first: knowledge is called practical principally from the end, praxis as end, and from the object only secondarily. The quidditative ratio of anything depends on its per se causes, each in its order; practical knowledge's per se causes include the end, indeed principally, and its end is praxis taken as per se, intrinsic, proper, and principal end.
claims: Practical knowledge is principally so from its end, praxis.
The end is a more principal cause than the object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1402.summary: Further: on their own view intellect and habit are practical from the same thing; the intellect is practical from the end, which is a more principal cause, since the end as loved or intended is the principle of the practical intellect (De anima III; Ethics VI, appetite is its principle), and the practical differs from the speculative by its end.
claims: Appetite for the end is the principle of the practical intellect.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1424.summary: Further: practical science is for the sake of work and per se ordered to it, and work is praxis, so practical knowledge is taken from praxis as end. It cannot be said that it is for work only accidentally and potentially because about the operable, since being about the operable and being for work differ, as do object and end. Aristotle says practical differs from speculative science by end, not object, else he would have distinguished them accidentally.
claims: Being about the operable differs from being for the sake of work.
Aristotle distinguishes practical and speculative by end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1450.summary: Further: by Ethics VI the good of the practical intellect is truth in conformity with right appetite, which holds only because practical knowledge takes its rule, measure, and first principle from right appetite for the end. Aristotle speaks of appetite of the end, not of choice following practical knowledge (as the Commentator says): right appetite and right reason are the two principles of choice. If it meant choice, there would be circularity among essentially ordered causes. So the appetite of the end grounds the truth and rule of practical intellect.
claims: Right appetite for the end is the rule and measure of practical truth.
Appetite of the end and right reason are the two principles of choice.
Reading 'appetite' as choice would make causation circular.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1500.summary: Further: that by approaching or departing from which rectitude and sin are measured is the first rule and measure of practical knowledge, and that is the end (Physics II).
claims: The end is the measure of rectitude and sin.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1513.summary: Further: as principles in speculative matters, so ends in practical (Physics II); practical knowledge is so from the end, not only the object, and depends on the end in being practical.
claims: Ends are to practical knowledge as principles to speculative.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1525.summary: Further: the first rule of practical knowledge and human acts is that by which a power commands all others; the will does this, since there are no human acts without its motion, and it has this from the end, corresponding to the universal end.
claims: The will commands all powers by virtue of the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1543.summary: Further: practical knowledge is properly called a rule by comparison to that by which something is knowingly right, and this is the end or appetite for it; knowledge has directive character only from the end, the first rule and principle the agent regards.
claims: Knowledge is directive only through the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1563.summary: Further, in truth (as in the next question): knowledge is not practical precisely from the object, since there can be speculative and practical knowledge of the same object, remote or proximate (praxis). Examples: theology of wayfarers, of the blessed, of God; our theology and Metaphysics XII about God; De anima III considering the act of will as object, which is speculative though there is also practical knowledge of it.
claims: The same object can be known speculatively and practically.
De anima's treatment of the will's act is speculative.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1592.summary: Further: practical science is active or factive (Metaphysics VI), which it has only from appetite and desire for the end, since the end is the moving principle.
claims: Being active or factive comes from desire for the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1603.summary: Further: the practical intellect and practical science say what is to be pursued or fled, and nothing is ever so called before appetite for the end.
claims: Judgments of pursuit and flight presuppose appetite for the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1614.summary: Further: knowledge is practical from the same thing by which an act is morally good or bad, which is principally the end, the principal circumstance in morals.
claims: The end is the principal moral circumstance.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1626.summary: A reason others add, of which the author is wary: the object relates to the habit as efficient cause and as terminus and end. Practicality is not from the object as efficient, since a habit caused immediately by God, not by the object, actually or aptitudinally, would still be practical or speculative, as with infused prudence and faith. So if from the object, it is as terminus and end, which grants the point. He does not rely on it, since by parity it would show practical knowledge is not from appetite for the end as efficient or naturally prior cause.
claims: Infused habits show practicality is not from the object as efficient cause.
This argument would prove too much.
concepts: object as efficient and as end

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1661.summary: Hence, the author says, infused prudence is not practical (as the next question will show for faith), since intellect and habit are practical principally from the end, not only from the object. The quidditative ratio and extension of practical knowledge depend on the end, praxis as end, more principally and distinctively than on the object, and more on praxis as end than as secondary object. So the practical intellect is called practical from the end or from being moved by appetite for it, since intellect and habit are practical from the same thing.
claims: Infused prudence is not practical, lacking dependence on appetite for the end.
Practical knowledge depends principally on praxis as end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1694.summary: Distinguishes kinds of extension of knowledge to praxis. One is possible extension, which can belong to purely speculative knowledge, the knowledge of the end preceding appetite for it.
claims: Purely speculative knowledge of the end can have possible extension to praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1705.summary: Another is actual extension, necessary to practical knowledge by common law (whatever God could do otherwise): the relation of actually practical knowledge to praxis formally, namely appetite for the end, as measured to measure, ruled to rule, posterior to prior, and as to an intended end, which may follow in reality, as many ends are prior in intention and posterior in execution. From this relation knowledge is called practical.
claims: Practical knowledge is constituted by its actual relation to appetite for the end as its measure and rule.
Ends can be prior in intention and posterior in execution.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1740.summary: The third is aptitudinal extension to subsequent praxis in reality, a relation of priority, direction, and conformation, so that executed praxis is posterior, directed, and conformed to practical knowledge. Knowledge is not called practical in act from this, since it is only aptitudinal, a relation of reason, sometimes actual when praxis exists but then accidental.
claims: Aptitudinal extension to subsequent praxis does not constitute practical knowledge.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1771.summary: Note for clarity: praxis as the end from which knowledge is practical can be taken in two ways. First, as intended and prior to practical knowledge, which is nothing other than love or appetite for the end, really a praxis whose object is the end. The end as loved is on its own side only a being of reason, while love of the end is real, and a being of reason is not truly a cause of real being, so practical knowledge depends rather on the love of the end. Everything said should be understood so.
claims: The end as intended is really the love or appetite of the end.
Practical knowledge depends on the real love of the end, not on the end as a being of reason.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1831.summary: Second, praxis as effected and directed by practical knowledge, concerning means; so taken it is not the cause or end of practical knowledge, being caused or directed by it. The praxis from which practical knowledge depends is praxis about the end or remote object (appetite for the remote end) or praxis about the end as intended. Knowledge relates aptitudinally to executable praxis as directive, but the relation by which it is practical is its conformity, as measured, to appetite or love of the end, on which the practical habit depends naturally; God could perhaps make the absolute practical habit without it. This is supported by De anima III, Ethics VI, and Physics II.
claims: Executed praxis about means is directed by, not causative of, practical knowledge.
Practical knowledge depends naturally on love of the end as its measure.
God could perhaps cause a practical habit without love of the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1905.summary: Note a special difficulty about speculative knowledge: it seems speculative neither from its end as achieved (posterior) nor from the end as desired (desire for truth need not precede it); so by parity neither should practical knowledge depend on its end. The reader should study and answer consistently. If a speculative habit depended on appetite for knowing, the end, that would be an act of intellect, per the description of praxis.
claims: It is difficult to see how speculative knowledge is so from its end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1927.summary: Whence an act is causally speculative seems to be not from its end or appetite, so from the object. Second note: the end of practical knowledge formally is always some praxis, as desired or intended by the knower, who acts only from appetite for the end; so practical intellect and formally practical knowledge presuppose appetite for the end, which is truly praxis. The apprehension of the end, even in particular, which directs that appetite, is not formally practical, since it precedes rather than depends on appetite for the end; it is purely speculative, a perfection of the speculative intellect.
claims: Speculative knowledge is so from its object.
Formally practical knowledge always presupposes appetite for the end.
Apprehension of the end preceding appetite is speculative, even if directive.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e1977.summary: Hence, though praxis can concern an end in particular such as God, there is no practical knowledge or practical intellect precisely about it preceding all praxis; formal praxis is simply prior in reality to formally practical knowledge. Unless one said that virtual precedence of praxis suffices (appetite for the end in common, in which there is no error), which would still keep practicality from the end. The earlier description, that praxis is posterior to intellection, applies universally only to intellection in common, not practical intellection; it is strictly true only of praxis about means. First intellection preceding appetite for the end can be called practical only possibly and denominatively, as directive of praxis about a particular end, but is purely speculative. Apprehension of the end in universal (good in common) is even less practical, preceding all appetite and not directive, since willing good in common admits no right or wrong.
claims: Some praxis is always prior in reality to formally practical knowledge.
Apprehension of the end, particular or universal, is speculative.
Willing the good in common admits no error and needs no direction.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2073.summary: Objection: knowledge of the end is like a principle to knowledge of means, a conclusion, and practical conclusions resolve into practical principles, so knowledge of the end is practical. Reply: it is never a principle of practical knowledge except through prior appetite for the end, which confirms the thesis. The paragraph ends by turning to the opposing arguments.
claims: Knowledge of the end is a practical principle only through appetite for the end.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2091.summary: Reply to the first argument for the object view: practical knowledge has no extension to work or practical ratio before appetite and intention of the end; all knowledge prior to actual appetite for the end is formally speculative. So practical knowledge could not exist naturally in an intellect separated from the will; positing it without appetite for the end would be positing a naturally dependent thing without its principle, making practical speculative and vice versa.
claims: Knowledge prior to appetite for the end is formally speculative.
Practical knowledge cannot naturally exist without the will.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2123.summary: Reply to the second: the end as intended, or rather the intention of the end, is a cause of practical knowledge; knowledge is not practical without the end first actually loved. It is practical from object, end, or both; not from the object alone, since the same object, such as God, can be known speculatively and practically (as intuitively and abstractively, and by intellect and will); so from the end, not the end in reality (posterior) but the end intended, or rather appetite for the end, necessarily and naturally prior.
claims: Intention of the end is a cause of practical knowledge.
The same object can be known speculatively and practically, so the object cannot be decisive.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2152.summary: Reply to the third: moral science is practical, and its end is the work of moral virtue. If all virtues are in the will, which is nobler than intellect, the argument from ignobility fails. If moral virtues are in sense appetite, or the will is less noble, the argument tells against Aristotle, who makes work the end of practical science. The end, especially the end 'by which', is not always nobler than what is for it; it suffices that it belong to the same person. Better: executed praxis is posterior and is not the principle of practical knowledge; the principle is love or intention of it, which belongs to the will and is nobler, even if the praxis belongs to sense appetite.
claims: The end of moral science is the work of moral virtue.
The end 'by which' need not be nobler than what serves it.
The principle of practical knowledge is the will's love of the end, which is noble.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2220.summary: Reply to the fourth: the first object of practical knowledge does not contain practical knowledge or principles without the intended end; they are taken from end and object together, principally from the end (Physics II, Ethics VI). A practical principle taken from the intended end is contingent, depending on the will's free appetite for the end. Yet the relations of practical knowledge to the intended end, and of praxis to practical knowledge for rectitude, are necessary, so a practical principle can be necessary; there are necessary relations among contingents. Speculative principles are not taken from an intended end and do not depend on the will.
claims: Practical principles depend on end and object together, principally the end.
Practical principles are contingent as depending on the will, yet include necessary relations.
There are necessary relations among contingent things.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2266.summary: Reply to the fifth: actual extension is not a per se attribute making knowledge practical intuitively and quidditatively; it is practical by its absolute nature. One who never actually intends work never has a practical act or acquires a practical habit, but a sleeping smith can retain a practical habit, since actual intention is required for the habit's acts and acquisition, not its conservation; a resting habit needs only habitual appetite. The same knowledge is never now speculative and now practical; one can have speculative knowledge of an operable object without intending the end and practical knowledge moved by desire of it.
claims: Actual intention is needed for acquiring and using a practical habit, not for retaining it.
The same knowledge never changes between speculative and practical.
One can have both speculative and practical knowledge of the same operable object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2329.summary: Reply to the sixth: the first, remote object of practical knowledge need not be operable by the knower: the lyre-player need not make the lyre, the rider cannot make the horse, the physician cannot make the body. So Aristotle's division by operable and non-operable objects is either particular, not universal, or concerns the proximate object, praxis, which is always contingent and operable by the knower. Praxis gives practicality more as end than as object.
claims: The remote object of practical knowledge need not be operable by the knower.
Aristotle's distinction by operable objects applies to the proximate object, praxis.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2390.summary: Reply to the seventh (Ethics VI): about contingent praxis freely elicited by the will there are contingent truths, belonging to the calculative part, and necessary truths (conditions for its rectitude), belonging to the scientific part. To Metaphysics VI: the inference 'science of eternal, immobile substance, therefore speculative' holds by reason of the matter, not universally or formally, since the remote object of practical knowledge need not be operable; it suffices that the proximate object be praxis. Or Aristotle presupposes truth as end. Or Aristotle followed his principles, not seeing that charitable love of God is the per se end of a science about God, needing it as directive, which, had he seen, he would not have so inferred.
claims: Practical knowledge includes contingent truths (calculative) and necessary truths (scientific) about praxis.
Knowledge of eternal substance need not be speculative.
Aristotle did not see that charitable love of God is the end of a science of God.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2469.summary: Fourth article: whether speculative and practical are essential differences of intellect and of knowledge.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2478.summary: First: speculative and practical together are not in the quidditative concept of the intellect absolutely and in common, else every intellect would be both regarding every object, and opposed differences cannot be in the concept of one per se being.
claims: Opposite differences cannot both belong to the quiddity of one being.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2507.summary: Second: neither one is in the per se concept of intellect in common, else every intellect would be practical or speculative regarding every object.
claims: Neither practical nor speculative belongs to the intellect's quiddity.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2520.summary: Third: they are not essential differences dividing the intellect as power into two powers. The intellect's adequate object is being, and it is not varied as power by variation of things under being, some ordered to appetite for the end, as sight is not varied by colours. And the higher and lower portions of reason vary only offices and acts, not the power (Augustine, De trinitate XII.4). So they are accidental differences of one power.
claims: Speculative and practical intellect are not distinct powers.
Higher and lower reason differ in office, not power.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2557.summary: Fourth: speculative and practical together are not in the quidditative concept of knowledge, habitual or actual, in common, as shown for the intellect.
claims: Practical and speculative together are not in the quiddity of knowledge.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2566.summary: Fifth: if speculative means the negation of relation to praxis as desired end and practical means that relation, they are not essential differences dividing knowledge, since knowledge in genus, species, and individual is something absolute and positive, and no relation or negation can be the separate or adequate differentia of an absolute positive. Also these presuppose the absolute natures of the knowledges as foundations, so cannot constitute them.
claims: Relations and negations cannot be essential differences of absolute natures.
Practical and speculative as relations presuppose the natures of knowledges.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2615.summary: Sixth: so taken, speculative and practical can be called distinct properties of knowledge: speculative belonging to one knowledge, to which the negation of relation to praxis as end belongs, practical to another knowledge differing in species, proximate genus, and individual, to which that relation belongs. They are per se inseparable attributes following these knowledges.
claims: Speculative and practical, as relations, are per se inseparable properties of distinct knowledges.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2639.summary: Alternatively, speculative and practical can be taken for the distinct intrinsic formal principles by which practical and speculative knowledge differ in proximate genus, species, and individual, which the relational properties follow. So taken they are specific and essential differences of knowledge in common, dividing it into subaltern species. Since practical knowledge in its whole genus has appetite for the end as per se cause and speculative does not, they differ specifically, and one can never become the other.
claims: As intrinsic formal principles, practical and speculative are essential differences of knowledge.
Practical knowledge has appetite for the end as per se cause; speculative does not.
A speculative habit can never become practical or vice versa.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2683.summary: Hence it is false, as some say, that the same habit can be now speculative and now practical by the arbitrary will of one intending or applying it to work or not; that is saying nothing. Ends the article.
claims: The same habit cannot change between speculative and practical by the will's choice.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2699.summary: Likewise false is the view that a habit is speculative in itself (from its object) but accidentally practical to its possessor, as is said of our theology of contingents, teaching about contingently right praxis like worshipping God at the altar. It is said to direct not from the object (rightly, since the divine object does not determinately contain such rectitude) but by supposition of God's will determining it. The author thinks this false: if it is speculative in itself it is so to its possessor, and if practical to its possessor then in itself, since practical and speculative divide habits per se, not accidentally.
claims: A habit cannot be speculative in itself yet accidentally practical to its possessor.
The rectitude of worship depends on God's will, not the divine object.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2741.summary: Reply to the first principal argument (from Metaphysics VI): clear from what has been said.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2752.summary: Reply to the second principal argument (Ethics VI on calculative and scientific parts): clear from what has been said.

qrdBas-a17109-d1e2760.summary: On De anima III (the practical object is the doable contingent good): false universally of the first object, but universally true of the proximate object, work or praxis, which is the end, and practical knowledge is taken more from it as end than as object. The Commentator on De anima III says the intellect by which we act differs from the speculative by its end, and on Metaphysics II that operative science, though reasoning about causes, is not speculative because it investigates causes and definitions in order to act, not to know.
claims: The doable good is the proximate object and end of practical knowledge.
Averroes distinguishes practical from speculative by end.

qrdBas-a17109.summary: Prologue q7 asks whether knowledge is called practical first and principally from its order to praxis as end or from its object. Bassolis first defines praxis, in agreement with Scotus. It is an operation of a power other than intellect, not cognition nor ordered to producing cognition, naturally posterior to intellection, in the knower's power, directable by right reason, and the per se, intrinsic, proper, and principal end of directive knowledge. Praxis is therefore an act of will, elicited or commanded, and willing God is per se praxis even without bodily acts. Against an opinion that the intellect is practical from the end and habits from their objects, he argues that intellect and habit are practical from the same thing. Against Scotus's view that knowledge is practical from extension to praxis as object, he argues that it is practical principally from the end, or rather from the real love or appetite of the end. That appetite is the rule and measure of practical truth (Ethics VI: truth in conformity with right appetite), the source of command, and the principal moral circumstance, and the same object (God, the will's act) can be known speculatively or practically. All knowledge preceding appetite for the end, including apprehension of the end in particular or in universal, is speculative, and infused prudence is not practical. He distinguishes possible, actual, and aptitudinal extension to praxis, and intended praxis (love of the end, which causes practical knowledge) from executed praxis about means (which it directs). A practical habit needs only habitual appetite to persist (the sleeping smith), and the remote object of practical science need not be operable (lyre, horse, body). Speculative and practical are not distinct powers or quidditative features of the intellect, which is one power like higher and lower reason. As relations they are inseparable properties of knowledges; as intrinsic formal principles they are essential differences, so no habit can switch between speculative and practical by the will's choice, or be speculative in itself but practical to its possessor. Aristotle did not see that charitable love of God can be the per se end of a science of God.
claims: Praxis is an act of will, elicited or commanded, directable by right reason and posterior to intellection.
Intellect and habit are practical from the same source.
Knowledge is practical principally from its end, namely the real appetite or love of the end, not from its object.
All knowledge preceding appetite for the end, including apprehension of the end, is speculative.
Speculative and practical are not distinct powers; as intrinsic principles they are essential differences of knowledge, and no habit can switch between them.
